frictionVectors.title: European gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control through Sonatrach and uses pipeline and LNG exports to preserve bargaining power with Europe. Demand volatility, infrastructure financing needs, and competition from other suppliers constrain leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign investment limits
frictionVectors.details: Local-content rules and political caution protect strategic assets but slow technology transfer and upstream investment. The hydrocarbons-heavy economy remains exposed to external price shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: Angola retains formal ownership of strategic resources, but public revenue and export earnings remain heavily dependent on offshore oil. Production decline and external financing pressures weaken sovereign room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed transport and energy projects have expanded connectivity while creating repayment and contractor-dependence concerns. Luanda is diversifying toward Gulf, Western, and domestic capital without fully displacing established ties.

frictionVectors.title: Cotonou strategic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Benin is strengthening the Port of Cotonou and logistics links to attract regional trade and investment, but relies on foreign capital, operators, and neighboring-market access. Disruptions in relations with Niger remain a major risk to transit revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence near the northern borders is testing state control over land, roads, and protected areas. Security cooperation with external partners is expanding, but dependence on outside training, equipment, and intelligence remains significant.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is using its diamond importance to secure greater domestic sorting, marketing, and beneficiation while preserving investor confidence. A prolonged downturn in global diamond demand could reduce the value of that leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-sector transition
frictionVectors.details: New coal, copper, and battery-mineral opportunities could broaden sovereign control over the resource base. Infrastructure costs, limited domestic processing capacity, and competition for foreign capital remain constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector control struggle
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking tighter state oversight of industrial and artisanal gold, challenging foreign operators and expanding public participation. Weak regulation, smuggling, and insecurity limit the state’s ability to capture full value.

frictionVectors.title: Security dependence and isolation
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou has reduced reliance on Western partners and expanded cooperation with Russia while distancing itself from regional institutions. This increases political autonomy but can worsen sanctions exposure, financing constraints, and infrastructure vulnerability.

highlights: Nickel and rare-metal ambitions attract external capital
Regional tensions constrain independent resource diplomacy

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions and Governance
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking investment in nickel, gold, and rare metals, but limited institutional capacity and opaque licensing risk leaving the state with weak bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda–DRC Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain strained, while instability in eastern DRC threatens trade routes, border security, and Burundi's room to pursue autonomous regional policies.

highlights: Stable maritime gateway with diversified external partnerships
Tourism and energy dependence limit strategic autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Atlantic Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde uses partnerships with the European Union, China, and other investors to expand ports, digital systems, and renewable energy, creating exposure to competing strategic interests.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country's position along Atlantic trafficking routes makes it reliant on foreign intelligence, patrol, and logistics support despite its efforts to strengthen sovereign maritime surveillance.

highlights: Oil, gas, timber, and mining remain state-controlled but externally financed
Conflict zones undermine infrastructure and territorial authority

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain important in roads, dams, mining, and construction, giving Cameroon infrastructure gains while raising concerns over debt exposure, contract transparency, and resource-linked concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone Conflict and Pipeline Security
frictionVectors.details: Separatist violence in the Northwest and Southwest disrupts transport and local economic control, while insecurity in the Far North and around energy corridors increases the cost of sovereign infrastructure management.

highlights: Russian security backing expands state reach while narrowing autonomy
Gold and diamond wealth remains vulnerable to informal extraction

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security and Mining Nexus
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel and commercial networks remain central to regime protection and access to mineral zones, creating a sovereignty trade-off between short-term security and control over strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: Informal Gold and Diamond Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Weak administration and armed-group influence enable smuggling through neighboring states, depriving Bangui of revenue and leaving foreign and regional intermediaries significant leverage over exports.

highlights: Oil revenue remains the core pillar of state financing
Post-transition diplomacy balances regional security and external partners

frictionVectors.title: Oil Dependence and Pipeline Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal sovereignty remains tied to oil production and export infrastructure linked to neighboring Cameroon, leaving the state exposed to price shocks, transit dependence, and unequal bargaining with international operators.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan War and Foreign Security Influence
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan conflict is driving refugee flows, arms risks, and border insecurity, while competing ties with Gulf states, France, Russia-linked actors, and Western partners complicate Chad's strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: FRANCE–MAYOTTE DISPUTE
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to contest French control of Mayotte, keeping sovereignty and migration issues at the center of bilateral relations. The dispute limits diplomatic room for deeper security and development cooperation.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on external partners for maritime, energy, and transport infrastructure. Competition among French, Gulf, Turkish, and other investors offers options but leaves national control over strategic assets limited.

frictionVectors.title: EASTERN CONFLICT AND REGIONAL INTERFERENCE
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and broader tensions with Rwanda continues to undermine Kinshasa's control over territory and mineral corridors. Regional security competition and illicit trade weaken the state's bargaining position.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL MINERALS GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: Cobalt, copper, and other strategic minerals attract intense competition from Chinese, Western, and regional actors. The government is seeking greater processing and revenue capture, but opaque contracts, smuggling, and weak enforcement remain major constraints.

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: State finances and elite power remain closely tied to offshore oil production, leaving national sovereignty exposed to price cycles and foreign energy firms. Diversification and domestic value addition remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: DEBT-FINANCED INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, public works, and energy projects provide critical capacity but increase dependence on external finance and contractors. Debt management constrains the government's ability to negotiate infrastructure terms from a position of strength.

frictionVectors.title: COCOA VALUE-CHAIN CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is pursuing greater local processing and producer protection, but multinational trading and chocolate firms still capture substantial value. Price volatility and sustainability rules imposed by external markets remain significant pressure points.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND SECURITY COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port and logistics expansion is attracting international capital while increasing competition with regional hubs. French, Chinese, Gulf, and other external partners remain important to infrastructure and security, creating manageable but persistent leverage risks.

highlights: Bases and ports sustain strategic leverage

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN BASE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its position at the Bab el-Mandeb through U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities. This generates revenue and diplomatic weight but makes national security highly dependent on external powers.

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEBT AND ASSET CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Large port and logistics projects have increased Djibouti's regional importance while exposing it to debt, concession, and ownership disputes. Competition between Chinese-linked infrastructure and Western-backed alternatives narrows the government's room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: NILE WATER SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam remains Cairo’s central sovereignty concern, with unresolved rules for filling and drought-time operations. Egypt is balancing diplomacy with regional pressure while protecting its agricultural water supply.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL FINANCING LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: IMF support and Gulf investment stabilize Egypt’s finances but increase outside influence over strategic assets, ports, and development priorities.

highlights: Gas monetization seeks a second wind

frictionVectors.title: MATURE OIL ASSETS
frictionVectors.details: Falling oil output and limited diversification are reducing state revenue and bargaining power. Offshore production remains dependent on foreign operators, technology, and capital.

frictionVectors.title: GULF OF GUINEA INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Malabo is promoting gas processing and maritime logistics, but project financing and foreign participation could leave strategic infrastructure externally controlled or commercially constrained.

frictionVectors.title: RED SEA MILITARIZATION
frictionVectors.details: Competition among regional and global powers for Red Sea access increases the value of Eritrean ports while intensifying pressure on Asmara to align with outside security agendas.

frictionVectors.title: ETHIOPIAN ACCESS PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia’s interest in reliable maritime access keeps the Eritrea-Ethiopia relationship strategically volatile. Port diplomacy remains tied to unresolved security and border concerns.

frictionVectors.title: REGIONAL REVENUE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on Southern African Customs Union receipts and regional supply chains, leaving fiscal sovereignty exposed to South African economic conditions and tariff shifts.

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY AND INDUSTRIAL BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Power reliability, logistics costs, and limited industrial diversification constrain domestic value capture. Foreign-owned firms retain significant influence in manufacturing and commercial agriculture.

frictionVectors.title: INTERNAL CONFLICT AND RESOURCE CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Continuing tensions in several regions complicate federal control over transport corridors, agricultural assets, and critical infrastructure. Security demands compete directly with development and debt-management priorities.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL FINANCE AND PORT ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia needs foreign capital and regional port arrangements while seeking to preserve strategic autonomy. Debt restructuring and Gulf, Chinese, and Turkish involvement create leverage over infrastructure choices.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining concessions
frictionVectors.details: The transitional government is seeking greater state participation and local processing in manganese and iron projects, creating tension with established foreign operators. Contract uncertainty could slow investment and exports.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gabon relies heavily on foreign-linked infrastructure and operators around Owendo and mineral corridors. Control of transport bottlenecks limits the state's ability to capture full resource value.

highlights: Cashew and groundnut value chains exposed

frictionVectors.title: Cross-border trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia's food, fuel, and transport security remain closely tied to Senegalese routes and market access. This dependence constrains independent bargaining over customs, transit, and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Port modernization pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign financing and operators are central to upgrades at Banjul Port and related corridors. Improved connectivity could raise state revenue, but also deepen external influence over strategic logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and mining governance
frictionVectors.details: The government is pushing tighter oversight, domestic refining, and formalization of artisanal mining, challenging entrenched foreign and local commercial interests. Illegal mining remains a major threat to land, water, and state authority.

frictionVectors.title: Critical minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Prospective lithium and other critical-mineral projects are attracting competing Western, Chinese, and regional interests. Ghana's fiscal constraints increase pressure to approve projects before building stronger domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou foreign consortiums
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore corridor is dominated by large international consortia and requires foreign capital, rail, and port infrastructure. Guinea can capture substantial rents, but remains vulnerable to external control of logistics and project timing.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite contract pressure
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are demanding more local content, infrastructure commitments, and revenue from bauxite operators, particularly those linked to China and the Gulf. Regulatory uncertainty and military rule raise the risk of abrupt contract disputes.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew export dependence
frictionVectors.details: Most cashew is exported with limited domestic processing, leaving producers and the state exposed to foreign buyers, seasonal financing, and price shocks. Attempts to raise local value addition face weak institutions and limited infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Bissau's port and maritime domain remain vulnerable to external commercial influence, smuggling, and narcotics trafficking. Weak enforcement reduces sovereign control over trade routes and complicates partnerships with Senegal and international security actors.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressure and reliance on international lenders limit Nairobi's freedom to set infrastructure and fiscal priorities. Chinese-financed projects remain strategically important even as Kenya seeks more diversified financing.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu port and transport corridor remain exposed to security risks and competition from established regional trade routes. Control over logistics, energy, and prospective mineral flows is increasingly contested by foreign investors and neighboring states.

frictionVectors.title: South African Water Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's hydropower and water exports provide essential revenue but deepen structural dependence on South Africa. Disputes over project financing, tariffs, and construction delays can constrain Maseru's negotiating autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Industrial External Ownership
frictionVectors.details: The garment sector depends heavily on foreign capital and preferential market access, especially to the United States. Changes in trade preferences or investor decisions can rapidly affect employment and fiscal stability.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gold, and prospective mineral projects are dominated by foreign operators, leaving Liberia reliant on concession revenue and export infrastructure. The government faces pressure to improve local processing, transparency, and fiscal returns.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Rail Access
frictionVectors.details: Control of railways, shipping terminals, and mineral corridors gives external firms significant influence over Liberia's trade architecture. Balancing investor demands with domestic access and revenue capture remains a central sovereignty challenge.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Control of Oil Institutions
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to contest access to oil facilities, budgets, and state institutions. Production disruptions and opaque revenue arrangements weaken national control over the country's primary resource.

frictionVectors.title: External Military Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed security actors and mercenary networks retain influence over bases, borders, and strategic infrastructure. Their presence reduces Libya's ability to independently secure energy corridors and manage migration routes.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining Chains
frictionVectors.details: Large nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mining operations depend on foreign capital, technology, and export markets. Madagascar captures revenue and jobs but remains vulnerable to price swings, contract asymmetry, and limited domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable power and weak transport links increase the bargaining power of external operators that finance dedicated roads, ports, and generation. This can isolate mining enclaves from broader national development and oversight.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Fiscal Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Malawi's fiscal space remains constrained by restructuring negotiations and dependence on international financial institutions. This limits policy autonomy over subsidies, public investment, and strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Minerals Investment Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Prospective uranium, rare-earth, and graphite projects are attracting foreign investors, but weak regulatory capacity creates risks of low domestic value capture and contested environmental terms.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Partnership
frictionVectors.details: The authorities rely heavily on Russian security support while seeking greater control over mining revenues and licenses. The arrangement may reduce Western leverage but risks opaque concessions and escalating sovereignty disputes.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-Sector Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is pressing foreign mining companies for higher state participation and revenue, creating legal and operational friction. Insecurity and transport disruption continue to threaten production and export routes.

frictionVectors.title: Greater Tortue Ahmeyim Gas Governance
frictionVectors.details: The offshore gas project with Senegal offers major fiscal and strategic gains, but cross-border revenue management and contract transparency remain sensitive sovereignty issues. Foreign operators retain substantial technical and commercial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Resource Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore rail and port infrastructure remain dominated by external capital and concentrated export routes. Fisheries access agreements and offshore energy development also generate recurring tensions over local benefits and control.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Settlement Implementation
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago has gained diplomatic momentum, but implementation of any UK agreement and the future of the Diego Garcia base remain strategically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: External Trade and Energy Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The island remains dependent on imported fuel, shipping connectivity, and external markets. This vulnerability is moderated by strong institutions, diversified services, and expanding renewable-energy investment.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is using ports, renewable energy, phosphates, and infrastructure investment to consolidate control and attract partners in Western Sahara. Polisario opposition and differing international legal positions remain persistent risks.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital in Strategic Sectors
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf, Chinese, and American investors are important to automotive, fertilizers, ports, and energy projects. Rabat is increasing local industrial content, but external financing and technology remain significant sources of leverage.

highlights: Cabo Delgado insurgency constrains state reach

frictionVectors.title: LNG and offshore gas leverage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led LNG projects dominate future export capacity, limiting Maputo's bargaining power despite increased state participation. Project timelines remain vulnerable to insecurity and contractor risk.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado security corridor
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent activity and dependence on foreign and regional security support expose weaknesses in sovereign control over the gas-producing north. Displacement and local grievances continue to undermine stabilization.

highlights: Green hydrogen strategy seeks local value

frictionVectors.title: Emerging offshore oil bargaining
frictionVectors.details: New discoveries could strengthen fiscal sovereignty, but foreign operators, financing, and technical dependence will shape how much value remains in Namibia. Expectations for rapid public benefits are rising.

frictionVectors.title: Green hydrogen infrastructure gap
frictionVectors.details: The hydrogen strategy requires major external capital, transmission, water, and port investment. Negotiating domestic processing and employment against investor demands is becoming a central sovereignty issue.

highlights: Junta asserts control over strategic resources
Western rupture raises investment and logistics risks

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and mining renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Niamey's effort to revise foreign mining relationships reflects a stronger sovereignty posture but risks reduced investment, legal disputes, and lower near-term production. Uranium exports remain exposed to transport and market constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Russian and regional security dependence
frictionVectors.details: The breakdown with France and wider Western partners has increased reliance on Russian-linked security support and alternative trade routes. This may expand political autonomy while narrowing financing and infrastructure options.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign oil capital versus national control
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria is seeking investment and higher output while renegotiating the role of international oil companies and managing subsidy, fiscal, and environmental pressures. Theft, sabotage, and weak refining capacity continue to erode effective resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-backed infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other external financiers remain important for rail, power, and industrial projects. These partnerships improve connectivity but create long-term repayment, procurement, and strategic-dependence concerns.

highlights: Regional security role carries economic costs

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda is positioning itself as a formal minerals-processing and trading hub, but international scrutiny over supply chains linked to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo threatens market access and reputational gains. Traceability remains strategically important.

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on external finance and security ties
frictionVectors.details: Aid, investment, and security partnerships support Rwanda's infrastructure and regional influence, yet restrictions or diplomatic pressure could narrow its room for maneuver. The country's assertive regional posture increases exposure to sanctions and conditionality.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Exploration Dependence
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe relies on foreign partners and licensing revenues for potential offshore oil development, while commercial discoveries remain uncertain. Weak administrative capacity limits its bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure and Tourism Finance
frictionVectors.details: The country remains dependent on external capital for ports, airports, energy, and tourism infrastructure, creating modest exposure to competing Chinese, European, and Gulf interests.

frictionVectors.title: Contract and Revenue Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing for greater national benefit from the Sangomar oil and GTA gas projects, creating tension with international operators and exposing fiscal and legal constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and Coastal Control
frictionVectors.details: Foreign industrial fishing and opaque licensing remain politically sensitive, particularly as coastal communities demand stronger protection of domestic access and marine resources.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles balances Indian, European, Chinese, and other maritime-security interests while seeking to preserve autonomy over its ports, exclusive economic zone, and surveillance infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and Climate Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on foreign tourism, imports, and external finance leaves the economy vulnerable to climate shocks, transport disruptions, and outside influence over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dominance
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mineral projects are central to growth but remain heavily dependent on foreign capital and operators, limiting domestic value capture and increasing concession-related tensions.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Road, port, energy, and digital projects require external financing, with Chinese, Gulf, and Western partners competing for influence amid tight fiscal conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Rivalries
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, and other external actors compete for influence over ports, logistics, and maritime security, while federal authorities struggle to align national and regional interests.

frictionVectors.title: Oil, Gas, and Territorial Disputes
frictionVectors.details: Emerging offshore resource activity is entangled with weak institutions, federal-state tensions, and disputes involving Somaliland and neighboring states, creating substantial risks to sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Beneficiation and Foreign Capital
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic processing of platinum-group metals, manganese and rare-earth inputs while balancing investment from China, the United States, Europe and Gulf states. Regulatory uncertainty and infrastructure bottlenecks limit Pretoria's leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and Port Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Transmission shortfalls, rail failures and congested ports continue to weaken state control over export-dependent mining value chains. Private power and logistics providers are gaining influence as public infrastructure struggles.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan remains dependent on Sudanese export infrastructure, leaving oil revenue vulnerable to conflict, sabotage and bargaining by actors outside Juba's control. Chinese and regional commercial interests remain deeply embedded in the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Elite and Armed-Group Competition
frictionVectors.details: Revenue, customs points and local resource access are contested among political elites and armed networks. Weak institutions make external security and commercial partners influential in determining how resources are extracted and transported.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Economies and External Patrons
frictionVectors.details: Gold remains a major source of war financing and is routed through opaque regional trading networks, including channels linked to Gulf markets. Competing foreign relationships are reinforcing rival military and commercial centers rather than national control.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Infrastructure Contest
frictionVectors.details: Port access, logistics corridors and prospective naval or commercial facilities on the Red Sea have become strategic bargaining assets. Foreign powers can gain leverage as Sudan's divided authorities seek financing, arms and diplomatic support.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Contract Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pressing for greater state participation, local processing and fiscal returns from gold, graphite, nickel and other strategic minerals. Negotiations with multinational firms remain sensitive as the government seeks investment without surrendering excessive control.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and Foreign-Financed Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Rail, port and corridor projects involving China, Gulf investors and other partners are expanding Tanzania's regional leverage but also create long-term exposure to external financing and operating interests. Dar es Salaam's role as a gateway increases the stakes of these arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Logistics Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's deep-water port remains central to Togo's trade and regional influence, with foreign shipping, finance and logistics firms holding substantial operational weight. Disruptions in the Sahel and Gulf of Guinea can quickly affect national revenue and supply security.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate Governance
frictionVectors.details: Phosphates remain a core strategic resource, but production and downstream value capture are constrained by financing, governance and infrastructure challenges. External investors are important to modernization, limiting the state's ability to dictate the full value chain.

frictionVectors.title: European Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia relies heavily on European financing, trade, and migration cooperation, giving Brussels substantial leverage over domestic and border policy. Fiscal pressure limits Tunis's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Import Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Declining domestic production and dependence on imported energy constrain sovereign economic policy. Phosphate-sector disruption further weakens export earnings and industrial resilience.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing
frictionVectors.details: The crude export pipeline and refinery strategy could expand Uganda's fiscal autonomy, but financing, sanctions pressure, and environmental opposition keep the project geopolitically exposed.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese contractors and lenders remain important to transport and energy projects, creating delivery capacity while increasing exposure to debt, procurement, and strategic-dependence risks.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Ownership Contest
frictionVectors.details: Lusaka is seeking more domestic value capture from copper and critical-mineral projects, while foreign investors retain strong influence over capital, technology, and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Power Supply Bottleneck
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower dependence and recurrent shortages threaten mines, manufacturing, and export reliability. Emergency imports and regional power deals reduce immediate risk but limit strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Lithium, platinum, gold, and other mineral projects attract Chinese, Western, and regional capital, but Zimbabwe still captures limited value beyond extraction and remains vulnerable to opaque contracting.

frictionVectors.title: Currency and Power Fragility
frictionVectors.details: Currency instability, electricity shortages, and sanctions-related financial restrictions weaken the state's ability to negotiate from strength with external investors and creditors.
